opus-5.5.text:
I think evaluations are probably one of the most underrated pieces of the whole picture. People tend to focus on compute, data, and architecture, and those obviously matter, but in practice what a model ends up being good at is very much shaped by what you can measure. If you can't evaluate a capability reliably, it's really hard to make steady progress on it, because you don't know whether a given change in data or training actually helped.

From my time working on Gemini and on reinforcement learning more broadly, a lot of the real work was figuring out what "good" even means for a given behavior. For something like math or coding, you have a relatively clean signal: the proof checks out, or the tests pass. That's a big part of why we've seen such fast progress there. But for things that are more open-ended, like being a genuinely helpful agent over a long task, or writing well, or exercising good judgment, the evaluation problem is much harder, and I think that's exactly where a lot of the differentiation between frontier labs comes from.

So my view is that evals aren't just a scoreboard you look at after the fact. They're closer to the steering wheel. The teams that invest in building really high-quality, hard-to-game evaluations that track what users actually care about are the ones whose models end up feeling noticeably better in practice, even when the benchmark numbers look similar. And as we move toward more agentic systems, that only becomes more true, because the space of behaviors gets so much larger and the cost of optimizing for the wrong thing goes up.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say evaluations are close to the center of it, and I think people outside the labs underestimate that. From the outside, progress looks like it comes from scale, from bigger models and more compute. That's real, but the thing that actually points the capability in a direction is the eval. You can't optimize what you can't measure, and in reinforcement learning especially, the eval and the reward end up being almost the same object. If you have a reliable way to verify that an agent did the task, you can train against it, and the model will get good at exactly that thing.

So the capabilities that distinguish frontier models today, long-horizon agentic work, coding, tool use, those are the areas where we figured out how to grade outcomes. The reverse is also true. The areas where models still feel weak are often the ones where we don't know how to write a good eval yet, where the task is open-ended or the judgment of quality is fuzzy. That's not a coincidence.

The hard part, and the part I think is underappreciated, is that building a good eval is a research problem in its own right. A benchmark that's easy to saturate or easy to game teaches the model to game it. You need tasks that are realistic, that have real signal, and that don't leak the answer. At Reflection, a lot of what we think about is exactly that question: how do you construct environments and verifiers that are faithful to the work you actually want the model to do. If you get that right, the model training almost follows. If you get it wrong, you end up with something that looks good on a leaderboard and falls over in practice.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes evaluations’ importance, but does not suggest that figuring out how to evaluate models is labs’ most important activity.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluations are incredibly important, because they define what you’re actually trying to get better at. You can have a very powerful learning algorithm, but if you can’t reliably distinguish a better outcome from a worse one, it’s hard to turn that into progress.

And there’s a difference between an evaluation that tells you where a model stands and one that helps you improve it. A benchmark might tell you that one model is a few points ahead of another, but it may not tell you why it fails on something you actually care about. For that, you need evaluations that capture the task and give you a meaningful signal when you make a change.

That becomes especially important as you move toward models doing longer tasks. Did it actually solve the problem? Did it recover when something went wrong? Those are harder things to measure than whether it produced the right answer to a short question. So I think the ability to measure progress well is a major part of the ability to make progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evaluations are incredibly important, because they define what you’re actually trying to improve. In pretraining, you have this very general objective: predict the next token. But as you move into reinforcement learning, you need some way to tell whether one outcome is better than another. And the quality of that signal has a huge effect on what the model learns.

Coding and math are good examples. You can run the code, you can check an answer, and that gives you a feedback loop. For something like doing research, it’s much harder to specify what success looks like. Is the idea novel? Is it correct? Does it actually matter? Those are much more difficult things to evaluate.

So I think a lot of the frontier is about figuring out how to measure the capabilities we care about. The catch is that an evaluation is always a proxy. You want to make sure that improving the score means the model is becoming more useful, rather than just becoming better at the particular test.
